zi: 'i' here sounds like [ɨ] (a buzzy apical vowel), not like the 'i' in 'bi'. The tongue tip stays flat behind the lower teeth.
ci: 'i' here sounds like [ɨ] (apical vowel) — the tongue tip is raised toward the alveolar ridge, creating a sibilant buzz.
si: 'i' here sounds like [ɨ] (apical vowel). The 'i' is merely a continuation of the 's' sound, not a separate vowel.
zhi: 'i' here sounds like [ʅ] (retroflex apical vowel). The tongue curls back toward the hard palate; it's not the front 'i' sound.
chi: 'i' here sounds like [ʅ] (retroflex). Air flows over the curled tongue tip, carrying the 'ch' sound into a sustained buzz.
shi: 'i' here sounds like [ʅ] (retroflex). The tongue curls back, producing a sound very different from the 'i' in 'xi'.
ri: 'i' here sounds like [ʅ] (retroflex). 'ri' is pronounced like the 'r' in 'run' but held as a sustained retroflex approximant.
ye: 'e' is pronounced like 'ê' [ɛ] (as in "bet"), not like [ɤ] (the usual 'e' sound). So 'ye' sounds like "yeh" not "yuh".
yan: 'a' is pronounced like 'ê' [ɛ] (as in "yen"), not the [a] of other 'an' syllables like 'fan'. The mouth is more spread.
yuan: 'uan' is pronounced like 'üan' [yɛn] — starting with a rounded front vowel, gliding to [ɛ], then [n]. Not "you-an".
yue: 'üe' is pronounced [yɛ] — a tight front rounded vowel gliding to [ɛ]. The 'e' is the open 'ê' sound.
yun: 'ün' is pronounced [yn] — a rounded front vowel [y] followed by [n]. The umlaut is dropped in writing after 'y'.
yin: 'in' is pronounced [in] (normal), but learners often confuse it with 'ying'. The difference is the presence of the velar nasal [ŋ] in 'ying'.
ying: 'ing' is pronounced [iŋ] — the vowel is slightly centralized before the velar nasal. Not "yeeng" or "yee-ng".
ju: Written 'ju' but pronounced 'jü' — the umlaut is dropped after j, q, x. The vowel is the front rounded [y].
qu: Written 'qu' but pronounced 'qü' — 'u' represents [y] (front rounded vowel) after q. Not [tʃʰu].
xu: Written 'xu' but pronounced 'xü' — 'u' represents [y]. The tongue position is the same as for 'xi' but with rounded lips.
juan: Written 'juan' but pronounced 'jüan' — 'u' is actually [y] + glide to [ɛn]. The umlaut is omitted by convention.
quan: Written 'quan' but pronounced 'qüan' — [tɕʰyɛn]. The 'a' is the open 'ê' [ɛ], not [a].
xuan: Written 'xuan' but pronounced 'xüan' — [ɕyɛn]. Same spelling rule as ju/qu/xu.
jun: Written 'jun' but pronounced 'jün' — [tɕyn]. The umlaut disappears after j, q, x.
qun: Written 'qun' but pronounced 'qün' — [tɕʰyn]. This is the same vowel as in 'yun'.
xun: Written 'xun' but pronounced 'xün' — [ɕyn]. Often confused with 'xiong' by beginners.
jue: Written 'jue' but pronounced 'jüe' — [tɕyɛ]. The 'e' is the open 'ê' [ɛ].
xue: Written 'xue' but pronounced 'xüe' — [ɕyɛ]. The [y] vowel requires active lip rounding.
iu: The final 'iu' is actually pronounced [iou] — there is a full mid-vowel glide between 'i' and 'u'.
ui: The final 'ui' is actually pronounced [uei] — the 'e' is audible in careful speech, giving "oo-ay".
un: The final 'un' is actually pronounced [uən] — there's a schwa [ə] between 'u' and 'n'.
bo: Despite being written 'bo', the pronunciation is [bwo] — a brief glide [w] appears between the initial and 'o'.
po: Pronounced [pʰwo] — a [w] glide appears between 'p' and 'o', making it sound closer to "pwo" than "poh".
mo: Pronounced [mwo] — the [w] glide is present after labial initials before 'o'.
fo: Pronounced [fwo] — like bo/po/mo, a [w] glide is inserted before 'o'.
lo: Pronounced [lwo] — an informal/rare syllable used in interjections like 'lo' (咯), with a [w] glide.
yo: Used in interjections like 'yo' (哟), with an 'io' final. The 'o' is [ɔ] rather than the usual 'o'.
dia: A rare syllable used in 'dia' (嗲) — the 'ia' final after 'd' is unusual in standard Mandarin.
nun: A rare syllable appearing in 'nun' (嫩 variant). The 'un' final surfaces with a clear schwa [uən].
m: Syllabic 'm' appears in interjections like 'm' (呣) — a standalone nasal without any vowel.
n: Syllabic 'n' appears in interjections like 'n' (嗯) — a standalone nasal. Often written as 'ng'.
ng: Syllabic 'ng' appears in 'ng' (嗯) — a velar nasal without any vowel. Used as a response sound.
hm: Syllabic 'hm' — an interjection with a voiceless 'h' onset followed by a nasal [m̥m].
hng: Syllabic 'hng' — an interjection with a voiceless 'h' onset followed by a velar nasal [ŋ̊ŋ].
bia: A rare/onomatopoeic syllable — 'ian' finals can shift after 'b' in character readings.
beng: The 'eng' final is pronounced [əŋ] — the vowel is a schwa [ə], not [e], giving a sound like "bəng".
peng: Same as 'beng' — 'eng' is [əŋ] with a centralized schwa vowel, not a front [e].
weng: The 'ong' final after zero initial becomes 'weng' [wəŋ] — the spelling shifts from 'ong' to 'weng'.
yong: The 'iong' final with zero initial is written 'yong' [jʊŋ] — the 'i' becomes 'y' and the vowel is slightly rounded.
